strengths: The authors presented an approach for multi-view representation learning.
In this framework, they combined together the advantages of the SpectralNet and the tricks of the graph Laplacian embedding for multi-view representation learning.
First, the approximate joint diagonalization of Laplacians is addressed mathematically, which opens the door to graph embedding from single view to multiple views.
Second, technically, they developed a metal learning model in terms of MLP to weight the single-view Laplacians.
The comparative experiments indicate the validity of the proposed framework.
The paper is well organized, the technical details are well described, and the writing is good for understanding.
The experiments are reported to support their main declarations.
SpecRaGE is a novel fusion-based multi-view spectral representation learning framework that effectively integrates graph laplacian methods with deep learning techniques.
Solves generalization and scalability challenges and is able to handle large data sets and generalize new samples.
Dynamic fusion technology is used to enhance the robustness of outliers and noise in contaminated multi-view data.
Achieved state-of-the-art performance in standard multi-view benchmarks, significantly outperforming existing methods when dealing with outliers and incomplete views.
SpecRAGE’s integration of graph Laplacian methods with deep learning for robust multi-view representation learning is a creative approach that addresses key limitations in handling noisy data.
The paper is clearly structured, with thorough experimental validation showing SpecRAGE’s effectiveness and performance advantages over state-of-the-art methods.
This paper is easy to follow.
This paper proposed a method that integrates the strengths of graph Laplacian methods with the power of deep learning.
The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
The paper is well organized, easy to follow. Problem statement is clear.
Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SpecRage in the face of noisy and outlier data.
weaknesses: The innovation of the framework is not distinctly significant, as it is largely constructed on existing works such as SpectralNet and approximate joint diagonalization of Laplacians.

The framework is developed on the existing SpectralNet from single view to multi-views. As an iterative approximation for intrinsic embedding in the work setting of deep learning, there is a gap in SpectralNet between those embeddings obtained from the graph Laplacian constructed on mini-batches and those obtained on the whole (global) dataset, which may cause the learned embedding to be far from that obtained strictly by traditional manifold learning approaches.

Figure 2 illustrates an example of visualization. It would be more important to visualize, simultaneously, the results obtained by the deep learning and those obtained by traditional manifold learning methods that are constructed on all of the data points.

It is necessary, theoretically or empirically, to demonstrate the power of the joint graph Laplacian by adding together (or in a linearly weighting way) all of the single-view Laplacian matrices; its algebraic meaning is actually not clear.

Although the authors claim robustness against outliers and noisy views, the experiments only add outlier and noise cases manually; evaluations on real‑world multi‑modal datasets would be needed to substantiate the claimed robustness.

Compared with the SOTA methods (like AECoKM and MetaViewer), the performances of the proposed SpecRaGE do not show significant enhancement; discussion of advantages in training/inference time, model complexity, or computation complexity is missing.
The framework as a whole is not end-to-end; some tricks could affect the final embeddings and require further discussion or future work.
There is no explanation of the newly introduced input character symbols in Figure 1, and the readability of the graph is not good.

The performance on a one‑million‑sample dataset (InfiniteMNIST) is similar to that on a 2k‑sample dataset (BDGP), yet no analysis is provided; moreover, the experimental data are not real contaminated data, creating a gap with real‑world situations and weakening the claimed effectiveness.
The selected comparative experiments lack representative significance; outdated methods from 2013 and 2015 are chosen without justification, leading to a serious lack of experimental analysis.

Formula specification problem: Using \mathcal{X} to represent the eigenmatrix is non‑canonical; variable notations such as lowercase v for the total number of views and lowercase q for the index of views are unusual and potentially confusing.

SpecRaGE’s approximate joint diagonalization may introduce cumulative errors when Laplacians are non‑commutative, affecting feature accuracy; it is unclear whether the authors have considered this issue.
The dynamic weighting module’s stability in high‑noise conditions is uncertain and needs testing under higher noise ratios.

The basis of weight generation by meta‑learning modules is not explained in detail; the definition of the weight vector w is missing, raising concerns about reliability when data quality differs significantly.
The baseline selection of the experiment is too old; more recent algorithms such as APADC or CPSPAN should be included for comparison.
The ablation experiment is not sufficient; it is unclear whether meta‑model weighting and view fusion are necessary.
This paper appears to be an incremental contribution, as it primarily combines graph Laplacian methods with deep learning techniques.

The authors claim to address generalization and scalability challenges, but the paper lacks substantial contributions in these areas; the generalization is achieved by a neural mapping function shared by most deep clustering methods, and scalability relies on stochastic mini‑batch training already introduced in SpectralNet.

The implementation of the meta‑learning approach is unclear; although a weight vector w_i is generated, the paper does not convincingly demonstrate a meaningful contribution to robust meta‑learning fusion.
A theoretical explanation for why dynamic fusion technology improves robustness against outliers and noise would strengthen the claim.
Assigning weights to a low‑quality view may reduce rather than eliminate noise impact, contrary to the intended robustness goal.
A visualization of the joint diagonalization structure would help readers intuitively grasp this concept.
Lack of Novelty: All proposed components are not new, and many similar frameworks have been proposed, such as [1].
Regarding the module of meta‑learning fusion, SpecRage simply uses learnable weights, which is similar to many existing works.
The SpecRage lacks ablation experiments to verify the effectiveness of each module.
